overview: If you only do one big paid day out in Cornwall, Eden is a strong contender, and it’s brilliant insurance against the weather. It’s built in an old china clay pit near St Austell that had been dug out for more than 160 years and was left with no soil at all. The charity behind Eden began turning it into a garden in the late 1990s, and it opened fully in March 2001.

What you’ll remember are the Biomes: two enormous domed greenhouses made of steel frames and hundreds of inflated hexagonal panels, one hot and steamy like a rainforest, the other warm and fragrant like the Mediterranean. Around them are roughly 30 acres of outdoor gardens. It’s all there to show how much people rely on plants, so there’s lots to read and look at, but you can just as easily wander and soak it up.
A lot of it is under cover, so it holds up well on a grey or drizzly day, but you do walk outside between the Biomes and gardens, and the site is on a slope, so bring a coat and comfy shoes.

expect.title: The Rainforest Biome
expect.text: Warm and humid, with paths that wind through tropical planting from Asia across to South America. You’ll see crops like rubber, sugar and cacao growing, walk through misty cloud and simulated downpours that show how rainforests make their own weather, and can climb to a viewpoint above the canopy. It gets hot in there, so wear layers you can peel off.

expect.title: The Mediterranean Biome
expect.text: A calmer, fragrant contrast to the rainforest, planted with Mediterranean-climate plants. One of Eden’s restaurants is inside, serving Mediterranean-style dishes, which makes a nice lunch stop.

expect.title: Outdoor gardens and play
expect.text: About 30 acres of gardens wrap round the Biomes, changing with the seasons, with art dotted about and places for children to let off steam, including water play when it’s warm.

expect.title: Free tours
expect.text: Guides run free daily tours of the Biomes; check the boards when you arrive for times. For something deeper there are paid, pre-booked experiences, such as a guided rainforest tour lasting a little over two hours.

expect.title: Winter extras
expect.text: From autumn into early spring there’s an ice rink, and around Christmas the Biomes open in the evening for a lights trail. Both need tickets on top of normal entry.

goodToKnow.label: Tickets
goodToKnow.text: Entry is paid, but a standard ticket lets you come back as often as you like for a year, so if you might return later in your week it’s already covered. Under-5s go free, there are discounts for Cornwall and Devon residents and for households on Universal Credit or Pension Credit, and booking online ahead is cheaper.

goodToKnow.label: Booking a time
goodToKnow.text: Annual and locals’ pass holders should book a time slot, especially in school holidays, and arrive within half an hour of it.

goodToKnow.label: Opening times
goodToKnow.text: Hours shift through the year, it’s closed on Christmas Day and some winter weekdays, and last entry is an hour and a half before closing.

goodToKnow.label: Parking
goodToKnow.text: Parking is free. At busy times a free shuttle bus runs from the car parks to the entrance, motorhomes are welcome, and there are paid electric car chargers. Use PL24 2SG in your satnav.

goodToKnow.label: Without a car
goodToKnow.text: Buses run from St Austell station, and Eden is on the National Cycle Network and the off-road Clay Trails if you fancy cycling in.

goodToKnow.label: Food
goodToKnow.text: Several cafés and restaurants cater for vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free diets. Bring a reusable cup for money off hot drinks; water refills are free.

goodToKnow.label: Route in
goodToKnow.text: Don’t let your satnav send you down the narrow lanes from St Blazey. Stick to the A391 and follow the brown signs.

setting.note: Two huge covered Biomes plus outdoor gardens

kids.note: Play areas, water play and family activities

entry.note: Tickets are sold on the official website

week.text: Give Eden most of a day and keep it up your sleeve for the wettest day of your week, when the beaches are a write-off. Because your ticket is valid for a year, you could also split it into two shorter visits. If you’re staying on the north coast it’s around an hour’s drive, so it suits a day based around St Austell Bay.

pairWith.why: a big, easy beach for a run-around afterwards
a historic harbour a short drive away for tea
if you’re garden people, the other big one is a few miles south

tips: Arrive early or after lunch: the middle of the day in school holidays is the busiest time.
Head into the Rainforest Biome first, before it warms up and fills up, then cool off in the Mediterranean one.
Bring a reusable water bottle; the free refill points are handy in the heat of the rainforest.
